# Job 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter
Bildad the Shuhite delivers his first speech. Unlike Eliphaz, who appealed to personal experience and private revelation (Job 4:12–21), Bildad appeals to **tradition and the wisdom of the ancients** (vv. 8–10). His theology is rigidly retributive: God unfailingly blesses the righteous and punishes the wicked. He is more blunt, less sympathetic than Eliphaz, and notoriously cruel when he suggests Job's children died for their own sin (v. 4). The speech is orthodox in its affirmations about God's justice but tragically misapplied to Job's situation.

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/
— Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

**v. 1 — "Then Bildad the Shuhite replied:"**
Bildad is the second of Job's three friends to speak. His name may derive from *Bel-dad* ("Bel has loved") or, as Keil & Delitzsch note, possibly *בל־דד* ("without breasts," i.e., brought up without his mother's milk), though nothing certain is known. Some think he was a descendant of Shuah, Abraham's son by Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2). Eliphaz had spoken first; Bildad now picks up the same line of argument. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html

**v. 2 — "How long will you go on saying such things? The words of your mouth are a blustering wind."**
Bildad opens harshly, without the courtesy Eliphaz showed. He accuses Job of being a windbag — vehement but empty. The Hebrew *כביר רוח* (poetical for "a great wind") conveys both the nothingness of Job's words and their blustering vehemence. Bildad hears Job's words but does not consider his pain. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm

**v. 3 — "Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?"**
Bildad's starting axiom: God cannot be unjust. This is the core of his (and all three friends') theology. The names used — *El* (the Mighty God) and *Shaddai* (the Almighty, All-Sufficient One) — emphasise God's power and self-sufficiency; such a God cannot be bribed or bent. The statement itself is true and would be blasphemy to deny. The problem is Bildad's insistence that this axiom explains *every* case of suffering. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm ; Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics): https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/8.htm

**v. 4 — "When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion."**
This is perhaps the cruelest line in the book. Bildad speaks conditionally ("if" / "when"), but his meaning is unmistakable: Job's children died because they sinned, and God justly gave them over to the destructive power of their own wickedness. Literally, "He sent them away by the hand of their transgression" — i.e., their sin became the instrument of their destruction. Bildad has no knowledge of the heavenly prologue (ch. 1–2) where God Himself declared Job's children blameless in the context of the test. As Andersen notes, "Job's children must have sinned. This is getting near the bone; for Job had been concerned about this very point and, by sacrifice, had provided against even their hidden sins." — Enduring Word (quoting Andersen, Smick): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/8.htm ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html

**v. 5 — "But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy,"**
Bildad softens slightly: there is still hope for Job (in distinction from his children, who are dead). The phrase "earnestly seek" translates *תשחר* — to seek early, diligently, with eagerness. Bildad urges Job to turn to God in humble supplication (*תתחנן*, to ask for grace/favour, not claiming merit). This echoes Eliphaz's counsel in Job 5:8. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm

**v. 6 — "if you are pure and upright, even now He will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate."**
Bildad's "if" is a veiled accusation: the implication is that Job is *not* pure and upright, since God has not yet delivered him. "Pure" (*זך*) and "upright" (*ישר*) are the very terms used of Job in the prologue (Job 1:1). Bildad unwittingly echoes God's own commendation while doubting its truth. "The habitation of thy righteousness" means Job's household, cleansed and justified from sin; God will restore and prosper it. The promise is beautiful — but it depends on a premise Job cannot accept without being untrue to his own conscience. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/8.htm ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm

**v. 7 — "Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish."**
Bildad promises that if Job repents, God will not only restore but increase beyond measure what he had. **Spurgeon** noted that Bildad meant this as a threat masquerading as encouragement — "he wished to prove that Job could not possibly be an upright man, for if he were so, his prosperity would increase continually." Yet Spurgeon also observed that Bildad's words turned out to be **prophetic**: "God put into his mouth language which did come true, after all… Job did greatly increase in his latter end" (Job 42:12). Spurgeon preached an entire sermon on this verse applying it to the spiritual life: the believer's beginning in grace may be small, but the latter end shall greatly increase. — Enduring Word (quoting Spurgeon): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Spurgeon Sermon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-beginning-increase-and-end-of-the-divine-life ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html

**v. 8 — "Please inquire of past generations and consider the discoveries of their fathers."**
Bildad shifts from direct accusation to an appeal to ancient tradition. This is his distinctive approach: whereas Eliphaz relied on personal visionary experience, Bildad relies on the accumulated wisdom of the ages. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 32:7 ("Remember the days of old; consider the years of many generations"). Bildad urges Job to "prepare himself" (*כונן*) — to apply his mind diligently to the research of the fathers. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm

**v. 9 — "For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow."**
Bildad shows a measure of humility: his own generation is ephemeral, of yesterday (*תמול*), lacking the long experience of the antediluvian patriarchs who lived centuries. Human life is "a shadow" — fleeting, insubstantial, dark, and quickly gone. This is the same imagery found in 1 Chronicles 29:15 and Psalms 144:4. **Clarke** noted a sundial motto: *Umbrae sumus!* ("We are shadows!"). Yet Bildad's humility is also a rhetorical move: by deferring to the ancients, he makes his argument seem unassailable. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm ; Enduring Word (quoting Clarke, Wiersbe): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 10 — "Will they not teach you and tell you, and speak from their understanding?"**
The ancients will speak "from their heart" (*מלב*) — i.e., from genuine, heartfelt conviction and understanding, not mere rote learning. The Hebrew *לב* here carries the sense of an intelligent, feeling heart (cf. Job 34:10, "a man of heart" = a man of understanding). Bildad is about to reproduce what he considers the distilled wisdom of the fathers, though the following proverbs may be his own composition in their spirit. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm

**v. 11 — "Does papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Do reeds flourish without water?"**
Bildad begins his series of nature-based proverbs. The papyrus (*גמא*) and the reed (*אחו*, an Egyptian loanword for Nile grass) cannot grow without their proper element — water and mire. The imagery is Egyptian, suggesting the poet's knowledge of Egypt and perhaps that Bildad views Egypt as the ancient source of wisdom. **Keil & Delitzsch** note that *גמא* derives from a root meaning "to suck up" (the papyrus is a thirsty plant), and that *אחו* is the Egyptian *akhi*, meaning "green, verdant." The principle: just as water is the necessary cause for reed-growth, so the favour of God is the necessary cause of human flourishing. Without God, the godless cannot truly prosper, whatever appearances suggest. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Peake's Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 12 — "While the shoots are still uncut, they dry up quicker than grass."**
The papyrus, though it grows tall and luxuriant quickly, withers even faster — "before all other grass," while still green and before it is ready for harvest. **Spurgeon** applied this to the hypocrite: "Long before the Lord comes to cut the hypocrite down, it often happens that he dries up for want of the mire on which he lives. The excitement, the encouragement, the example, the profit, the respectability, the prosperity, upon which he lived fail him, and he fails too." — Enduring Word (quoting Spurgeon): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html

**v. 13 — "Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish."**
This is the application of the papyrus simile. "The paths of all who forget God" — like wind-swept tracks in the desert that disappear (cf. Psalm 1:6). The "godless" (*חנף*) is the hypocrite or the secretly wicked — one whose outward righteousness masks inward corruption. Their hope "perishes" — the Hebrew *תאבד* suggests going under, being lost entirely. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/8.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 14 — "His confidence is fragile; his security is in a spider's web."**
The Hebrew literally reads "whose confidence is cut off" (*יקוט*), and "whose trust is a spider's house" (*בית עכביש*). A spider's web is formed with great art and industry, yet is slender, feeble, and easily swept away. **Poole** noted: it "may do much mischief to others, yet is most slender and feeble, and easily swept down or pulled in pieces, and unable to defend the spider that made it." The same image appears in the Qur'an (29:40): "Verily the frailest of houses is the spider's house." — Enduring Word (quoting Poole): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Peake's Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-8.html

**v. 15 — "He leans on his web, but it gives way; he holds fast, but it does not endure."**
The godless man rests his full weight on what cannot support him. The "house" (a play on the spider's "house" = web) collapses when leaned upon. The repetition ("leans… gives way" / "holds fast… does not endure") underlines the utter futility of false security. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/8.htm

**v. 16 — "He is a well-watered plant in the sunshine, spreading its shoots over the garden."**
A third natural image — a luxuriant climbing or creeping plant, full of sap, green before the sun, spreading its branches over the garden. **Ellicott** sees this verse as the start of a contrasting picture of the *righteous* man (not the wicked), marked by an emphatic pronoun in Hebrew: "Green is *he* before the sun… quite unlike the watery paper-plant." However, most other commentators (Keil & Delitzsch, Gill, Enduring Word) see this as continuing the description of the wicked in his temporary prosperity — a plant that seems luxuriant but has no lasting root. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/8.htm ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 17 — "His roots wrap around the rock heap; he looks for a home among the stones."**
The plant's roots intertwine around a heap of stones; it "looks upon a house of stones" — i.e., regards the stony structure as its own, as though it had taken possession of a durable house. But stones offer no nourishment, only the illusion of stability. The godless man treats his fortune as a solid, imperishable structure. **Keil & Delitzsch** reject the reading "he splits stones apart" (Ewald) or "he strikes against a layer of stones" (Rosenmüller), insisting *בית* ("house of stones") means the plant twines itself about a stone wall and looks proudly upon it. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/8.htm

**v. 18 — "If he is uprooted from his place, it will disown him, saying, 'I never saw you.'"**
The one who casts away is God (not the stones). Once uprooted, the place that seemed to belong to him disowns him entirely — it denies ever having known him. This is total erasure: the once-flourishing plant leaves no trace, and the place itself testifies against him. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 19 — "Surely this is the joy of his way; yet others will spring from the dust."**
"This is the joy of his way" is deeply ironic — "so fashioned, so perishable is it, so it ends" (Keil & Delitzsch). The prosperous course of the godless comes to this. Others will spring up from the same dust to replace him, their fate no different if their confidence is equally misplaced. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 20 — "Behold, God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers."**
Bildad recapitulates his core conviction. "The blameless" (*תם*, *tam*) is the very word used of Job in Job 1:1 — Bildad is making a pointed reference. "Nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers" — literally, God does not "take by the hand" (i.e., support, uphold as His own; cf. Isaiah 41:13) those who do evil. **Andersen** observes: "In his simple theology everything can be explained in terms of two kinds of men – the blameless (*tam*, Job 8:20a; used of Job in 1:1) and the secretly wicked (*hanep*, Job 8:13b). Outwardly the same, God distinguishes them by prospering the one and destroying the other." This is the retributive dogma in its purest form. — Enduring Word (quoting Andersen): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/ ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Precept Austin (James Smith): https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith

**v. 21 — "He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy."**
Bildad closes with a promise: if Job repents, God will turn his mourning into laughter. The language echoes Psalms 126:2 ("Then our mouth was filled with laughter"). **Ellicott** renders it "he will yet fill thy mouth with laughter — afflicted though thou hast been, thou shalt again rejoice." Bildad means this conditionally (if you repent), but — like v. 7 — the promise proves truly prophetic, for Job's end is indeed filled with joy and restoration (Job 42:10–17). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/8.htm ; Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

**v. 22 — "Your enemies will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."**
Bildad refers to Job's adversaries as "those who hate you" (*שנאיך*), a term that may subtly include himself and the other friends — or at least shows he still tries to think the best of Job. "Clothed with shame" (cf. Psalm 35:26; 109:29; 132:18) and "the tent of the wicked will be no more" form a final, psalm-like note of warning. Bildad has done all he can to win Job over — but his counsel, though orthodox in content, is fatally misapplied, for it rests on the false premise that all suffering is punitive. — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

---

## Protestant Traditions: Points of Distinctive Emphasis

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
Spurgeon treated Bildad's words as the uninspired reasoning of a mere man — "they spake as men — as mere men… not to be accepted as being inspired" — yet he found gospel truth in them nonetheless. He preached a full sermon on v. 7 ("Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase"), applying it to the spiritual life: the believer who starts with small grace need not fear, for "the beginning of the godly and upright man may be but very small, but his latter end shall greatly increase." He urged anxious beginners to take comfort, and used the sermon to confirm faith, quiet fears, and quicken diligence. He also used vv. 11–18 as a detailed portrait of the hypocrite — the reed that grows quickly, is hollow, easily bent, and bears no fruit. — Spurgeon Sermon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-beginning-increase-and-end-of-the-divine-life ; Enduring Word (quoting Spurgeon): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

### Reformed / Evangelical (broadly)
The consistent Reformed and evangelical reading sees Bildad as the archetypal "ramrod traditionalist" who reduces God's ways to a mechanical cause-and-effect formula. **Keil & Delitzsch** articulate the theological error precisely: "It is true that nothing that God sends to man proceeds from injustice, but it is not true that everything that He sends to him comes from His justice." God's attributes (justice, mercy, love) are not all in operation on the same object at the same time. Bildad's mistake is thinking his "commonplace utterance is sufficient to explain all the mysteries of human life." **Precept Austin** likewise notes that Bildad had "made an incorrect connection between a righteous life and material prosperity — the same mistake that Satan had made (Job 1:9–11)." — Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/job-8.html ; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_devotionals-2

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
**David Guzik** (Enduring Word) emphasizes that Bildad and the other counselors "talk a great deal, but what they do not do is pray. It would seem that Bildad had very little real experience with God; yet Job was being prepared to experience God so intimately that he could say, 'now my eyes see You' (Job 42:5)." Guzik draws a contrast between theology as a belief system and genuine experiential knowledge of God — a characteristically charismatic emphasis. He also highlights **Oswald Chambers'** insight that "if you take an illustration from Nature and apply it to a man's moral life or spiritual life, you will not be true to facts because the natural law does not work in the spiritual world." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

### Anglican (Ellicott)
**Ellicott's Commentary** (Charles John Ellicott was an Anglican bishop) offers a distinctive reading of vv. 16–19. While most commentators see these verses as continuing the description of the *wicked* man as a luxuriant but doomed plant, Ellicott argues (based on the emphatic Hebrew pronoun) that v. 16 begins a contrasting portrait of the *righteous* man — "green is he before the sun, quite unlike the watery paper-plant." The righteous man's roots are wrapped around a perennial spring; his luxuriance is genuine, not apparent. Ellicott acknowledges this reading is debated but defends it on grammatical grounds. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/8.htm

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
**Peake's Commentary** notes that Bildad's speech contains Egyptian vocabulary (*אחו*, the Nile grass, an Egyptian loanword *ahu*), suggesting that "the poet was acquainted with Egypt" and probably "means to represent Bildad as viewing Egypt as the source of the oldest Wisdom." Peake also observes that "the two younger friends… make a less favourable impression than Eliphaz" and that Bildad's "whole idea of fortune and misfortune is even more mechanical than that of Eliphaz." — Peake's Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-8.html

**Dr. Constable's Expository Notes** characterize Bildad as "objective and analytical… a neat but superficial thinker. He is a moralist, and in his simple theology everything can be explained in terms of two kinds of men — the blameless and the secretly wicked." Constable also notes the poignant irony that "Bildad's assertion that God will not reject a blameless man (v. 20a) makes him the precursor of those who mocked Jesus with the same logic: 'He trusts in God; let God deliver him' (Matthew 27:43)." — Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-8.html

### Catholic and Orthodox
No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Job 8 was retrievable from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the available searches.

### Debated Popular Teachings (Prosperity Gospel)
The book of Job as a whole stands as a powerful corrective to any "prosperity gospel" teaching. Bildad's theology — that righteousness guarantees material prosperity and that suffering proves sin — is precisely the error that the whole book refutes. **Precept Austin** explicitly states that Bildad "had made an incorrect connection between a righteous life and material prosperity. In fact, it was the same mistake that Satan had made (1:9–11)." God Himself rebukes Bildad and the other friends in Job 42:7: "You have not spoken of Me what is right, as My servant Job has." The prosperity hermeneutic is here shown to be both theologically inadequate and pastorally cruel. — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_devotionals-2 ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-8/

---

*Sources consulted: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott's Commentary, Gill's Exposition, Keil & Delitzsch, Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics), Peake's Commentary, Dr. Constable's Expository Notes, Spurgeon's Sermons, Precept Austin (including James Smith notes). Catholic/Orthodox and Lutheran sources were not retrievable within search limits.*
